sentences.text: Revenue, net interest income plus noninterest income, rose from $21.0 billion in FY2016 to $28.5 billion in FY2025, a 3.5% CAGR [D5][D219].
The path was a step change rather than steady compounding: revenue was $22.7 billion in FY2021 and $28.0 billion in FY2023 [D117][D169].
FY2023's 15.8% revenue growth came from higher rates on earning assets and the MUB acquisition, partly offset by deposit mix and pricing [D189][P33].
FY2025 revenue grew 4.4%, with net interest income up 2.2% on loan growth and lower deposit rates and noninterest income up 7.6% across most categories [D239][D234][D235][P16].
Consumer and Business Banking was the largest segment at 31.0% of FY2025 revenue but shrank 3.9%, subtracting 1.3pp from growth [D251][D252][D253].
That decline came from deposit mix and second-quarter loan sales, which cut segment net interest income 4.9% [P6].
Payment Services grew 5.4% in FY2025 and contributed 1.4pp, on 25.8% of revenue [D260][D261][D259].
Payment Services net revenue rose on higher loan balances and lower funding costs, plus merchant processing and card revenue from higher sales volume [P4].
Operating costs fell 2.0% while revenue grew 4.4%, so operating costs fell 6.4pp more than revenue [D238][D239].
The FY2025 efficiency ratio of 59.0% sat below its 59.3% window median and well below the 67.4% FY2023 high [D220][D277][D276].
The ratio improved from 62.9% in FY2024 as noninterest expense fell 2.0%, reflecting prior-year merger and FDIC special-assessment charges and lower compensation [D195][D220][D238][P10].
The credit-loss provision was 7.7% of revenue in FY2025, above the 6.1% peer median [D221][D285].
Net margin of 26.5% sat 31.8pp below the 58.3% net interest income share of revenue, with the provision and expense the gap [D223][D222].
Operating cash flow is not a meaningful earnings-quality measure for a bank, so capital return is the better test [F60].
Buybacks plus dividends of $3.66 billion were 48.3% of FY2025 net income of $7.57 billion [D218][F30].
Buybacks fell from $2.56 billion in FY2016 to $489 million in FY2025, while dividends rose from $1.81 billion to $3.17 billion [X76][X85][X86][X95].
The diluted share count fell 9.6% over the window, from 1,724 million to 1,558 million, so EPS grew faster than net income [X66][X75].
Return on average equity was 12.2% in FY2025, above the 11.8% peer median and in the 71st percentile of seven banks [D226][D283][D282].
Loans were 73.5% of deposits and the allowance 2.0% of loans, against 80.5% and 1.6% in FY2016 [D224][D225][D10][D11].
Long-term debt was last reported at $39.8 billion in FY2022 and is not reported after that year [F104][X172].
That break limits any read on leverage trends after FY2022, so the equity build to $65.2 billion is the cleaner capital signal [F114].
Long-term debt is not reported after FY2022, a data gap flagged as high severity [R2][X172].
The gap matters because debt-funded balance-sheet growth cannot be separated from deposit and equity funding in later years [R2].
Revenue declined in FY2024, with net interest income down 6.4% on higher rates pressuring deposit mix and pricing [R1][D194][D209][P21].
That decline reversed in FY2025, so it reads as a rate-cycle swing rather than a persistent erosion [D239].
If the FY2026 efficiency ratio rises above the 59.0% FY2025 level, the cost trend described here would be reversing [D220].
If net interest income growth falls below the 2.2% FY2025 rate, the loan-growth and funding-cost tailwind would be fading [D234].
If the credit-loss provision rises above 7.7% of revenue, credit quality would be deteriorating from the FY2025 level [D221].
